summary.text: A male term newborn delivered at 40 weeks weighing 3620 g with Apgar scores of 8 and 9 had respiratory distress a few hours after birth, treated with noninvasive oxygen support and empirical ampicillin and gentamycin. He was admitted at 2 days of age with significantly elevated inflammatory markers and concern for neonatal sepsis.

Workup showed leukopenia (WBC 4.05 x 10^9/μl), significant neutropenia (ANC 0.01 x 10^9/μl), CRP 92.5 mg/L and procalcitonin 53.9 ng/mL, Escherichia coli from the pharyngeal swab, Enterococcus species from the eye swab, and a negative blood culture; the antibiotic regimen was revised to include meropenem, amikacin and local ciprofloxacin for blepharitis. Immunoglobulin levels, normal lymphocyte subpopulations and an ultrasound screening without associated congenital abnormalities were also reported.

He had delayed separation of the umbilical cord stump with erythema surrounding the umbilicus, treated with local antibiotics and surgical ligation. Serial blood counts showed persistent neutropenia and monocytosis; bone marrow aspiration at 3 weeks of age showed maturation arrest of myeloid cells at the myelocyte stage without excess blasts.

Genetic analysis revealed a novel heterozygous ELANE c.200C > G (p.Ser67Trp) mutation, classified as pathogenic and de novo, with no pathogenic variants in other SCN-associated genes, confirming severe congenital neutropenia.

He was discharged on the 34th postnatal day clinically stable with advice to continue oral antibiotics and antifungal prophylaxis, and attended regular outpatient checkups where persistent neutropenia and monocytosis were noted. At 3 months he was readmitted for an abdominal wall skin lesion treated with parenteral antibiotics, which resolved.

He received prophylactic sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim and nystatin from the parents, had no serious bacterial infections noted and normal growth and development, and G-CSF was started at approximately 1 year of age at 5 μg/kg/day and gradually increased, with a mild sustained ANC increase up to 0.8 x 10^9/μl over 6 months of follow-up.

article_limitations: Figure pixels are inspected in the separate visual submission; the caption-layer visual status stays not_inspected.
Table 1 literature rows and the discussion of 27 published cases describe other patients and are not attributed to the index patient.

Figure 1 prints 56 exact values (WBC, ANC, monocytes, Hb on 14 dated tests, 2/2/2024 to 5/3/2024); they are transcribed in the visual submission, not duplicated as annotation facts, and the chart dates are not linked to postnatal days by inference.
Case text calls the abdominal wall lesion painless and the Figure 3 caption calls it tender; both are kept as source conflicts.
Text writes 10^9/μl for WBC and ANC while the Figure 1 key gives 10³/uL; units kept as written.
